state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it in terms of baking. If you were making cookies and doubled all the ingredients, would the size of the cookies change? Think about how changing the heights of the plants would affect the overall range.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if you double all the ingredients the cookies get bigger, so yeah the range would change... but I'm still confused about Katie's one though - if you just add 3 cm to each plant, does that actually change the range or not?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it in terms of a race. If every runner in a race runs 3 meters further, does that change the distance between the fastest and slowest runner? Think about how adding 3 cm to each plant would affect the overall range.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I get it now - if every runner runs 3 metres further, they all still finish in the same order and the gap between them stays the same, so adding 3 cm to each plant wouldn't change the range either. So does that mean Katie is right and Tom is wrong then?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses well-chosen analogies to help the student reason through both multiplicative and additive transformations, successfully guiding them from their initial misconception to the correct understanding that only additive changes preserve range.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (baking cookies, runners in a race) to help the student understand abstract mathematical concepts about range, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
